The five judgements that move the shares, and the arithmetic if each judgement is wrong

Even the most favourable single judgement leaves FY2027 EPS at about 4.45, far below consensus at 6.08; the FDA date is the swing factor for FY2028. All sensitivities below are on FY2027 unless stated, and they start from the model's base: revenue 1,162; EBITDA 279 (a 24.0 percent margin); D&A 120; net financial items -8; a 20 percent tax rate; 31.6 million shares; EPS 3.82. The sensitivities assume no cost response, because management has said that investment continues.

1. The largest lung customer's step-down: Viewforth assumes revenue from the customer falls by 65 in 2027, within a plausible range of 40 to 100. The customer, Lung Bioengineering (part of United Therapeutics), provided 132 of Xvivo's 2025 revenue. Lung Bioengineering built about 10 of inventory in Q3 2026 ahead of running its own approved ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) platform, although STEEN Solution and some components stay inside that platform. DNB Carnegie's estimate of 5 to 6 percent of 2027 revenue is the only published sizing, and the company has not quantified the step-down.

The arithmetic for each 35 of lost revenue runs as follows. The lost revenue is kits and services at about 75 percent gross margin, so 35 of revenue is 26 of gross profit. With no cost offset, 26 of gross profit is 26 of EBITDA (about 2.2 points of margin) and 26 of EBIT, because amortisation is unaffected. After 20 percent tax, 26 of EBIT is 21 of net income, or about 0.65 of EPS over 31.6 million shares. A fall of 100 therefore puts FY2027 EPS at about 3.2 and leaves lung revenue flat on the year; a fall of 40, which is 25 better than the base, puts FY2027 EPS at about 4.3.

2. The European heart ramp: Viewforth assumes heart revenue of 155 in 2027, up from about 90 in 2026, within a plausible range of 120 to 190. RedEye now dates the first CE-marked commercial invoices to December 2026, so the commercial clock for the heart system starts in Q1 2027. France reimburses the heart system, and the Netherlands, Austria, Belgium and the United Kingdom are negotiating reimbursement. The sell-side sits at about 180 to 194, near the top of the plausible range.

The arithmetic for each 35 of heart revenue: at an 82 percent thoracic gross margin, 35 of revenue is 29 of gross profit; after about 4 of variable selling cost, it is 25 of EBITDA and 25 of EBIT; after tax it is 20 of net income, or about 0.63 of EPS. Heart revenue of 190 gives FY2027 EPS of about 4.45 and matches the sell-side's revenue line; heart revenue of 120 gives FY2027 EPS of about 3.2. Heart revenue at the sell-side's level also matters beyond EPS, because it would let management keep its 2027 targets as an "ambition" at the Q4 report rather than re-date them.

3. Operating-cost growth: Viewforth assumes operating costs excluding depreciation grow 13 percent to about 562 in 2027, and the risk to that assumption is one-sided. Cost growth of 15 to 17 percent is as likely as cost growth of 11 percent. In 2026, cost growth of 14 percent absorbed almost all of the revenue growth: the underlying incremental EBITDA margin in Q3 2026 was about 15 percent once the 19 of timing items are removed. In 2027 the cost base carries 10 to 13 United States commercial hires, launch preparation and a surgical roster hired ahead of volume.

The arithmetic: cost growth of 17 percent means costs of 582, which is 20 above the base, and gives EBITDA of 259 (a 22.3 percent margin), EBIT of 139, net income of about 105 and EPS of about 3.3. Cost growth of 11 percent (costs of 552) gives EBITDA of 289 (a 24.9 percent margin) and EPS of about 4.1. A spending pause like the one in H2 2025 would add three to four points of margin within two quarters, but I do not count such a pause as upside, because using it would signal that the launches had failed.

4. The FDA's handling of the heart PMA: Viewforth assumes approval in late 2028 and a United States launch in Q1 2029, a judgement that moves FY2028 rather than FY2027. My probability distribution for the approval date is about 15 percent by end-2027, about 35 percent in H1 2028, about 30 percent in H2 2028 and about 20 percent for 2029 or a request for further data.

The arithmetic for approval in H1 2028 with launch in H2 2028: about 100 of United States heart revenue in FY2028 at an 80 percent gross margin adds 80 of gross profit. The launch organisation's cost is already in the base, because Viewforth's costs grow 22 percent in 2028 whether or not the revenue arrives, so EBITDA also rises by 80. Amortisation of the PMA asset (about 350 over ten years, or 35 a year) starts a year earlier, so EBIT rises by about 55 after a part-year charge, and net income rises by about 43 after 21 percent tax. The result is about +1.3 on FY2028 EPS of 6.07, and the launch-year build of working capital also moves forward. In the opposite case, a request for further data removes about 50 of Continued Access and preparatory revenue, capitalisation of development continues for another year or two (a cash cost, not an EBITDA cost), and FY2028 EPS falls to about 5.0. In either direction the effect on the share price dwarfs the effect on EPS, because the approval date decides whether consensus FY2028 EPS of 9.5 to 10.5 survives.

5. The krona: Viewforth assumes USD/SEK averages about 9.0 to 9.2 in 2027, and the krona is the widest single contributor to the EPS range while having nothing to do with the operating case. About 55 percent of Xvivo's sales are in dollars and 35 percent in euros, against a largely krona cost base and with no hedging; in addition, about 250 to 300 of cash is revalued through financial items. A 10 percent move in the dollar changes sales by about 45 and EBITDA by about 16 (two margin points) through trading, and changes financial items by a further 25 to 30 through the revaluation of cash. The total is roughly 40 of pre-tax profit, 32 after tax, or about 1.0 of EPS. The consensus macro path is a headwind: Intesa Sanpaolo forecasts USD/SEK at 9.15 by end-2026 and 8.67 by late 2027, down from 9.70 in mid-2026, and a Riksbank rate rise is likely in November 2026. A dollar at 8.5 takes FY2027 EPS to about 3.1; a dollar holding at 9.6 lifts FY2027 EPS to about 4.3.

A sixth item moves estimates without changing the business: aligning the sell-side to the disclosed amortisation and a normal tax rate takes 8 to 10 percent off FY2027 consensus EPS before any operating number changes. The CE-mark asset alone amortises at 39 a year, whereas DNB Carnegie models 38 of total development amortisation for 2027; Viewforth uses a 20 percent tax rate, whereas DNB Carnegie models 15 percent through 2028. The alignment will happen piecemeal: the Q4 report will show 9.75 of CE-mark amortisation in a single quarter, and the annual report in March 2027 will show the tax note.

1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

The demand tailwind is structural, external and strengthening: three forces raise demand for organ perfusion independently of anything Xvivo does.

  • The donor mix. Donors after circulatory death (DCD) reached about half of United States donors in 2025 and grow over 7 percent a year. DCD organs need machine assessment: 55.8 percent of United States DCD donors underwent normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) in Q1 2026.
  • The regulation of organ procurement. A Florida federal court upheld the rule of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) on 28 September 2026. The rule ranks organ procurement organisations (OPOs) in three tiers and exposes Tier 3 OPOs to decertification, which starts in late 2026; current OPO agreements expire in January 2027. Underperforming OPOs must pursue marginal organs, and marginal organs create perfusion demand.
  • Hospital staffing. Over 76 percent of surveyed hospital executives report shortages of perfusionists and surgeons, and those shortages pull organ evaluation into centralised hubs. Hubs are the route Xvivo has built: three OPO hubs are active against a target of four to five, and OneLegacy's hub, opened in July 2026, serves over 70 transplant centres.

Competitor growth proves that the demand force is sector-wide. TransMedics grew 37 percent in 2025 and its services grew 29 percent in Q2 2026; Terumo's Organ Technologies unit (OrganOx) grows 39 to 50 percent, and Terumo raised its guidance in August 2026; Paragonix grows 65 percent organically under Getinge. The addressable market is estimated at USD 2.9 billion by 2033, growing about 7 percent a year, with penetration at about 4 percent and unmet need at ten times supply.

Regulators have been the largest single positive of the last six months. The heart system received its CE mark; France granted national reimbursement (18 May 2026); the FDA received the heart PMA, with Breakthrough designation and an expanded Continued Access Protocol with CMS cost recovery; Health Canada approved Xvivo's liver and kidney systems; and Bridge to Life's January 2026 clearance created a 510(k) predicate for hypothermic liver perfusion, which let Xvivo replace a 215-patient trial with a 510(k) submission in H1 2027.

The headwinds are real, and they are concentrated in price and in one customer.

  • Price competition has risen in every organ except lung fluids. Getinge bought Paragonix (at 11x sales) and Terumo bought OrganOx (at about 20x). Bridge to Life cleared its VitaSmart liver system at USD 15,000 to 20,000 a case, against about USD 30,000 to 45,000 for OrganOx and USD 80,000 to 100,000 for TransMedics; Bridge to Life then raised USD 110 million in August 2026 and won funding for the category from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). In an October 2026 interview, a surgeon described a centre that runs 95 percent of its normothermic liver cases on OrganOx because of cost.
  • The largest lung customer has become a competitor (judgement 1).
  • Cost caps penetration. United States lung EVLP is still only 10 to 20 percent of transplants after a decade; expert testimony caps it at 20 to 30 percent on current economics; a full XPS run costs about USD 40,000; and 90 percent of United States centres use free cold storage for standard-risk organs.
  • Supply problems raised costs and cut margins in 2026. Kidney growth slowed to 19 percent in Q3 from 72 percent because a component must be replaced until early 2027; inventory was written down; and the manufacturing transfer from the Netherlands to Sweden completes only in Q4 2026.
  • Tariffs touch the European-made heart, liver and kidney disposables; the lung consumables are made in the United States.
  • The macro regime works against the security rather than the business: a United States ten-year yield near 5.1 percent, a market that "refuses re-ratings", monetary tightening in Sweden and a stronger krona (judgement 5).

Inference and so-what: volume is the reliable leg of the case, and price is not. Industry adoption compounds steadily and has two-plus years of visibility, but Xvivo's capture of that adoption is lumpy. Xvivo's quarterly revenue growth went -15, -5, -1, +10, +34 and +34 percent on a flat end market, because one customer destocked and then restocked and heart sales under derogation (special national permission before the CE mark) rose from 9 to 24 a quarter. The external forces justify revenue growth above 20 percent a year. The external forces do not by themselves deliver the margin targets, because the same forces that lift volume also commoditise abdominal pricing: when hospital budgets are flat, the cheapest adequate system wins.

Where my view differs from the market. The market reads the OPO rule and the rising DCD mix as unqualified tailwinds. I agree on the direction and add that the OPO transition will disrupt contracting for about two quarters around January 2027 before it accelerates demand, which is one reason Viewforth's Q1 2027 growth is only 14 percent. The market also treats the lung customer as an item worth 5 to 6 percent of revenue. I treat the customer's range (a fall of 40 to 100) as the widest operating uncertainty of 2027 and the most likely source of a negative surprise, because Xvivo discloses nothing about the contract, the fluid volume per run or the price.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the "cheapest adequate system wins" pattern spreads from liver to lung, as hospital-built extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) circuits and the customer's own platform erode the price of Xvivo's lung products. Two events would change my view: a second large lung centre seeking approval for its own platform, or a volume-tied STEEN discount to the largest customer, which would be the first real price concession in lung fluids.

Score: 60. A strong, structural and externally driven demand tailwind with two-plus years of visibility, partly offset by rising competition, a customer turning supplier, a penetration ceiling set by cost and an unhedged krona in a tightening Sweden.

2Internally driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

The heart programme is the largest product entry in Xvivo's history, and its clinical evidence is the strongest in its category.

  • Europe: in commercial launch. Eight centres use the heart system under derogation, and a three-tier rollout prioritises about 30 centres with funding pathways in France, the Netherlands, Austria and the United Kingdom.
  • United States: under FDA review. The PRESERVE trial enrolled 141 patients five months early and showed 92.1 percent 30-day success and 91.4 percent one-year survival.
  • Evidence: randomised and linked to survival. The NIHP2019 trial showed a 76 percent reduction in severe primary graft dysfunction and one-year survival of 92 against 86 percent. NIHP2019 is the first randomised heart-preservation trial linked to survival, and it was published in The Lancet and the European Heart Journal.
  • Adoption precedent. Australia reached 40 to 50 percent penetration of brain-death heart transplants under special access, which shows what supported adoption can reach.

The other programmes and the organisation have also moved forward. The liver route pivoted to a 510(k) submission, which is a year earlier and far cheaper than the trial it replaced. Kidney has approval in Canada and a broader United States launch in 2027. The tenfold disposable-capacity project (about 50 of capital) completes in Q4 2026, with abdominal manufacturing consolidated in Sweden and a target abdominal gross margin of 70 percent. The H2 2025 cost and cash programme produced a record 25 percent EBITDA margin in Q4 2025 and four consecutive quarters of positive operating cash flow. Rolling forecasts replaced annual budgets; the United States field force was restructured toward the South and West; the April 2026 annual general meeting added two independent directors with United States commercial experience; and the long-term incentive plan now rewards perfusion-volume growth of at least 12 percent a year.

The problems are specific, and four of them matter.

  • Services. Services revenue fell 28 percent organically in Q3 2026 at a -19 percent gross margin, the sixth quarter of decline, and management says contracts "are taking longer than originally anticipated".
  • The chief financial officer (CFO) seat. The finance director was redeployed on 1 April 2026 to run strategy and the services unit, and the CFO seat has had no named successor for eight months in the most launch-intensive year in the company's history.
  • FlowHawk and morale. FlowHawk's growth fell to 0 percent in Q3 from 48 percent without explanation, and the employee net promoter score fell from 51 to 27 in 2025.
  • Guidance and amortisation. There is no numerical guidance in a year with three launches, and the nine-month capitalised development of 131.7 (37.1 for heart in Q3 alone) becomes amortisation, starting with 39 a year for the CE-mark asset.

Every regulatory date before the two that landed this year slipped: the CE mark slipped by six to twelve months on a component change, and United States kidney slipped from 2025 to 2027. There is no change of chief executive, no pricing lever, no capital return and no reduction of the business perimeter; the company is adding lower-margin activities (NRP and hub operations) rather than exiting the one activity that loses money.

Inference and so-what: Xvivo is running a launch programme on top of an external demand inflection, not a transformation. The programme's strength is concentrated in the thoracic product line, where Xvivo's advantages are deepest. The programme's weakness is that the same internal forces keep launch costs high through 2027 and add a loss-making services node, which is why Viewforth models costs growing 13 percent in 2027 and about 22 percent a year in 2028 and 2029. The internal forces justify revenue growth above 20 percent for three years, and they defer dependable conversion of that growth into earnings to 2028.

Where my view differs from the market. The sell-side treats the services unit either as launch infrastructure (RedEye) or as a drag (DNB Carnegie); I treat the unit as small either way, at about one point of group margin. I treat the CFO vacancy as the under-discussed execution risk, because one executive carries finance, strategy, business development and the services turnaround while the sell-side models the company without guidance. The market has not noticed FlowHawk's stall. The stall is immaterial to revenue (the acquisition cost 57), but a goodwill impairment of 50 to 100 is a 2027 to 2028 risk to reported, though not adjusted, earnings.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that staged, careful execution is exactly what a company with no United States commercial record should do, and that the pace will prove right. Three events would change my view upward: a permanent CFO who sets a margin floor; a capital-markets day with a bridge from EBITDA to EPS; and disclosed hub throughput above about 150 EVLP runs a year. One event would change my view downward: a services gross margin still below -10 percent in Q1 2027 with no contract conversions.

Score: 58. The heart launch is a genuine, well-resourced and sensibly staged change force and the liver pivot is smart, but there is no guidance, no leadership change, a failing services leg and an unfilled CFO seat.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

The industry structure supports Xvivo completely in lung, substantially in European heart and liver, and contests Xvivo in every United States organ it is entering. Each organ is a near-monopoly behind regulatory and switching-cost barriers: Perfadex holds about 90 percent of static lung preservation; LifePort holds about 95 percent of United States kidney perfusion; TransMedics holds 40 to 75 percent of United States liver perfusion and handles 21 percent of all United States transplants through its National OCS Program (Organ Care System), with 22 aircraft and over 1,000 heart cases; Liver Assist holds over half of European liver perfusion. Share in lung fluids has not moved in two decades. Share in the device layer moves 10 to 20 points in two years wherever a cheaper adequate device appears, as OrganOx showed, and as Bridge to Life showed by moving from clearance to NICE funding and a USD 110 million raise in eight months.

Competitors at the top of each market put margin first, while entrants put volume first. TransMedics is the unstable actor: a founder-led company that absorbed a short-seller attack in January 2025 and a 25 percent share-price fall on its May 2026 miss, that attacks cold perfusion publicly, and that launched its CHOPS product to block rivals.

Xvivo's business model has one deep and widening moat, in lung, and an untested advantage in heart. The lung moat combines proprietary fluids, clinical evidence and an installed base that compounds: machines at USD 500,000, kits at USD 40,000, and FlowHawk in six of the ten largest United States transplant programmes. The moat earns thoracic product gross margins of 80 to 85 percent, which held at 84 percent through the inflation of 2023. The heart system enters with the category's best evidence at a third of the incumbent's price, a real advantage on paper that remains untested in the United States, the market that matters.

Three advantages are absent. Xvivo lacks scale (207 employees and no volume discounts from suppliers). It lacks an owned logistics network: it rents logistics through partners, namely 175 perfusionists via Perfusion Solution Inc, five aviation companies and the OPOs. And it lacks pricing power outside lung: the abdominal gross margin fell from 68 percent in Q2 2025 to 54 to 57 percent in H1 2026 on mix and "temporary price pressure", before recovering to 61 percent in Q3. The addressable market allows revenue growth of 20 to 25 percent for four years without heroic share assumptions; the constraints on growth are the cost of reaching the market (selling expenses are about 37 percent of sales) and the timing of approvals, not the size of the market.

The financial profile is above average at the gross line and below average everywhere beneath it.

The earnings base is not clean. The 20 percent EBITDA margin would be near zero if the roughly 175 a year of capitalised development were expensed, which is why the Industry Digest names Xvivo, alongside Coloplast and GVS, as a "false friend". Against the four peers in the peer table, Xvivo has the highest revenue growth, but Bonesupport shows what a delivering Nordic single-product medtech earns: an EBITDA margin of 29 to 35 percent and free cash flow of 0.8 to 1.5 times net income.

Management is a careful, honest and scientifically excellent steward with a demonstrated weakness in United States commercial execution.

  • For. Christoffer Rosenblad, chief executive since November 2022 and an internal successor, doubled revenue from 415 to 822 in two years, ran the heart trial to completion early, delivered the CE mark and the PMA filing, and restored cash generation with the 2025 programme. He communicates honestly: he announced the CE-mark delay proactively, warned investors against extrapolating the 25 percent margin quarter and disclosed the Q3 timing items unprompted.
  • Against. TransMedics out-executed Xvivo in the United States for a decade; the services unit lost accounts to physician-led teams; management misjudged the 2025 destocking, which produced a 30 percent one-day share-price fall; employee sentiment halved during scaling; and capital allocation is reinvestment without demonstrated returns (the STAR Teams acquisition cost 22 to integrate and created the loss-making services unit, and management describes FlowHawk only as "an option").
  • Governance. Governance is clean: a single share class, six of seven directors independent, executive pay that fell 18 percent in 2025 on missed targets, and warrants that expired unexercised. The flags are structural rather than behavioural: the chairman is dependent on Bure, the 14.27 percent shareholder; insider ownership is thin; and there is no internal audit function.
  • Ambition and pace. Management's ambition is large in words ("standard of care for all donor hearts"; "2027 as a springboard to 2028") and measured in pace, so Viewforth models the company's commercial dates with a lag of two to four quarters.

Inference and so-what: hold the thoracic margins, cap the abdominal recovery, and treat management's United States execution as the judgement that matters most for 2028 to 2030. Viewforth holds thoracic product margins at 80 to 85 percent through the horizon; treats the recovery of the abdominal margin as an execution outcome capped in the low-to-mid 60s through 2027; assumes no pricing tailwind outside the heart's conversion from compassionate to commercial pricing; and treats returns on capital as an output of the margin path rather than a constraint on it. The model asks for about 90 of United States heart revenue in 2029, less than TransMedics' OCS Heart achieved in its first full year, so that figure is a floor rather than a stretch.

Where my view differs from the market. The bull case rests chiefly on the strategic-buyer multiple of 11 to 20x sales. I use that multiple as a floor for the equity, not as support for the earnings, and I note that the floor is untested while Bure controls the nomination committee. The market also treats the heart system's clinical superiority as settled. I note three cautions: the earlier European cold-heart trial failed its endpoints; a surgical-research director argues that the ice comparator inflated the measured benefit; and no multi-year head-to-head data exist. United States share gains should therefore be modelled centre by centre and made conditional on registry data.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case, which is also the leadership digest's own conclusion, is that a Swedish consensus culture cannot out-execute a hyper-aggressive United States competitor and that an all-organ launch exceeds the organisation's capacity. Three events would change my view upward: the naming of the United States heart launch organisation and its owner; reimbursement decisions in two Tier 2 countries by April 2027; and services at breakeven. One event would change my view downward: a surgeon-led defection in European heart to Paragonix's static container on price.

Score: 50. A sector-leading franchise and clinical record in lung and heart, a strong balance sheet and honest management, set against low returns on capital, an unclean earnings base, no scale, contested abdominal pricing and a decade of being out-executed commercially in the United States.

4Conservatism of guidance, expectations management, and the record of delivery

Xvivo gives no numerical annual guidance and never has; its forward statements are of three kinds, and none of them is conservative.

  • The 2027 targets: an EBITDA margin above 30 percent, an EBIT margin above 20 percent and an abdominal gross margin of 70 percent. Management reaffirmed the targets in July 2026 after a 6 percent EBITDA miss and restated them at Q3 without new numbers.
  • Dated operational milestones: a United States heart launch "targeted" for end-2027 "subject to FDA review and approval" (narrower wording than before); the liver 510(k) submission in H1 2027; kidney growth resuming in early 2027; four to five hubs; and tenfold capacity by Q4 2026.
  • One quantitative steer: in July 2026, management said FY2026 EBITDA would be in line with consensus, which then stood at 206.

Management set the 2027 targets before the services unit turned loss-making, before the customer's platform approval and before the CE-mark amortisation was known. Every broker now sits below the targets: for the 2027 EBITDA margin, DNB Carnegie is at 25.0 percent and RedEye at 23.4 percent after Q3, and Viewforth is at 24.0 percent.

The record against the sell-side is one of revenue beats, profit misses and slipped dates. Sales beat consensus in four of the last five quarters (by 4, 4, 2 and 6 percent). EBITDA beat twice (Q4 2025 by 31 percent; Q3 2026 by 14 percent) and missed twice (Q1 and Q2 2026, by 6 percent each). Over twelve months, consensus FY2027 EPS has been cut 13 percent while consensus revenue was held, and FY2026 EPS has been cut 21.5 percent, while FY2028 EPS was raised 7 percent: the near years have been cut and the far year raised. Every regulatory date slipped before the two that landed this year. The company publishes a compilation of consensus before each report (on 19 October for Q3; the next precedes the report of 28 January 2027), so beats and misses are well defined. The company's qualitative commentary (services slow; kidney constrained; margin partly seasonal; investment continues; sales to the largest customer to decline) has been the accurate half of its communication, and that commentary is more cautious than consensus for the next twelve months.

Inference and so-what: the targets work as ambition rather than as a guidance floor, so the sell-side, not the company, will drive any upgrade cycle. Xvivo has no mechanism for raising anything, and the sector rewards the first beat-and-raise, which a company that does not guide cannot deliver. The honest reading is an archetype: Xvivo is a company that lowers expectations qualitatively when it must and never raises them numerically. The figure above gives my probabilities for the next 18 months; in addition to a re-dating, the targets could be reframed or dropped. The FY2026 EBITDA steer should be met approximately: Viewforth has 199, against the post-Q3 brokers' 199 to 200.

Where my view differs from the market. The sell-side has already discounted the targets, so a re-dating is a small event for estimates; retail investors hold the targets as a promise, so a re-dating is a larger event for the narrative. The market misses a constructive reading: a company that resets its targets once, at a credibility low, has every incentive to set the new target where it can beat it. A re-dating to "above 30 percent by 2029" would therefore be a negative headline and a positive setup, whereas a reaffirmation in January 2027 would be a neutral headline and a negative setup for January 2028.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that Q4 heart revenue above 30 and two Tier 2 reimbursement decisions would let management keep the targets credibly, and that the sell-side's 2027 margin of 23 to 25 percent is already the effective guidance. Either a capital-markets day with a numerical bridge or the company's first numerical annual guidance would change my view and move this score by 15 to 20 points.

Score: 28. No numerical guidance, stretch targets that every broker discounts and that will be re-dated, a record of revenue beats but profit misses and slipped dates, and an upgrade cycle that only the sell-side can start.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost control and feedback loops

Operating leverage is large and demonstrated, and management has switched it off by choice. With a gross margin of 70 to 74 percent and an operating-cost base excluding depreciation of about 496 (50 percent of sales) that is mostly people, each point by which revenue growth exceeds cost growth adds roughly 0.7 points of EBITDA margin. The record shows the leverage working in both directions:

  • FY2024's incremental EBITDA margin was 44 percent on extra revenue of 224.
  • Q2 2025's 15 percent revenue fall took the EBITDA margin down to 13 percent.
  • Q4 2025's spending pause produced a 25 percent margin.
  • Q3 2026's reported incremental margin was 25 percent, but about 15 percent underlying, because hiring absorbed the growth.

Viewforth models an incremental margin of about 45 percent from 2027, the 2024 pattern, which lifts the EBITDA margin from 20 percent to 24 percent in 2027 and to 31.5 percent by 2030 while costs still grow 13 to 22 percent a year. About a fifth of the incremental EBITDA is absorbed by amortisation of the assets that made the launches possible. As a result, EBITDA grows about 3.6x over FY2026 to FY2030 (from 199 to 709) and EBIT grows about 4.4x from a much lower base (from 114 to 504), but EPS grows only about 3.1x (from 3.93 to 12.18) once the tax rate normalises.

Pricing power is applied in lung and given back in abdominal, and it adds almost nothing after 2027. Lung consumables hold their price: an increase of about 5 percent in the United States in November 2025 offset tariffs and the weak dollar, and Medicare's reasonable-cost pass-through for organ acquisition insulates the purchase from hospital budgets. However, real price growth in lung is zero, and management describes STEEN at about USD 7,000 a litre as "the limit". The one real price event is the heart system's conversion from derogation pricing to commercial pricing after the CE mark. The conversion is worth 20 to 40 percent per case on the existing eight-centre volume, or about 20 to 30 of 2027 revenue at nearly full margin, and it is a one-off step rather than a trend.

Real abdominal prices fall 1 to 2 percent a year against VitaSmart and OrganOx. The recovery of the abdominal gross margin from 59 percent in FY2026 to 63, 66, 68 and 69 percent is therefore an outcome of unit cost and mix, not price: the Swedish consolidation lowers unit cost, with savings lagging by one to 1.5 years because Xvivo receives no volume discounts. Nordic precedents for manufacturing transfers suggest 2028 is when the savings show: Ambu's move to Mexico cost 1.5 points of margin dilution and took about three years to reach cost parity. In net terms, price adds about one point to 2027 revenue growth and half a point to the 2027 gross margin, and nothing thereafter.

Three identified efficiency bridges are worth five to six points of EBITDA margin by 2029, and Viewforth models about four points arriving, weighted to the later years. A fourth bridge reaches cash rather than EBITDA.

The true cost-cutting lever, a spending pause like the one in H2 2025, releases three to four points of margin within two quarters, and it belongs in a downside case only.

Financial leverage is nil; the amplifier of earnings is currency. Net interest is within plus or minus 3 a year, and there is no deleveraging, buyback or dilution effect (incentive plans dilute by at most 1.35 percent). Judgement 5 sizes the krona at about 1.0 of EPS per 10 percent move. Net financial items swung from +112 in 2024 (including 59 of contingent-consideration revaluation and a large exchange gain) to -50 in 2025 (including a currency loss of 66.6) and to about +30 in the first nine months of 2026.

Two reinforcing feedback loops drive revenue, and 2027 is the one year in which the balancing loops are as large as the reinforcing ones in lung. The lung hub-and-spoke loop works as follows: more hubs bring more spoke centres, more EVLP runs, more consumables and more evidence, and United States EVLP disposables grew 56, 69 and 183 percent through the quarters of 2026. The heart clinical-network loop uses 15 European trial sites, about a quarter of European heart centres, as reference centres. The balancing loops are customer insourcing and the national reimbursement calendars. In 2027, lung revenue excluding the largest customer grows 25 to 30 percent, but the customer's step-down and the Q3 2026 timing items remove about 85, so lung revenue grows only about 8 percent, and the heart loop has not yet compounded. A third loop, capitalisation, reverses on approval: reported EBITDA funds capitalised development, which sustains reported EBITDA, until approval turns the capitalised cost into amortisation, so cash improves and reported profit worsens at the same time. From 2028 the reinforcing loops dominate, and revenue growth re-accelerates to 27 and 25 percent.

Where my view differs from the market. The sell-side's framework is the "EBITDA margin trajectory": the brokers model the leverage (26.8 percent for 2027 before Q3; 23 to 25 percent after Q3) but do not model management spending it through 2027. The market also credits "operating leverage" without separating the mechanical part (lung volume and heart mix, which I credit) from the discretionary part (hiring, which management has said continues). I agree with the market that EBITDA margins above 30 percent are attainable for a consumables business with product margins above 80 percent. The peer set says that reaching such margins takes a launch cycle, not a year: Ambu took two to three years to add ten points, and TransMedics approaches a 30 percent operating margin only by 2028, after a decade.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the Q4 2025 quarter showed that the cost base can be held flat at will, and that a permanent CFO would impose that discipline in 2027. Two readings would change my view: operating costs excluding D&A below 135 a quarter in Q4 2026 with revenue growth intact, or an abdominal gross margin at or above 64 percent in Q1 2027.

Score: 58. Top-decile gross margins and demonstrated operating leverage mean revenue growth will produce outsized profit growth from 2027 to 2030, but the leverage is being spent by choice through 2027, pricing power exists only in lung, there is no financial leverage, and the krona adds as much EPS variance as the operating case.

6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and higher growth and margins than the past

Viewforth's forecasts compound revenue at about 23 percent a year and triple EPS from FY2026 to FY2030, yet sit 36 to 41 percent below consensus EPS from FY2027 onward.

The segment build shows heart rising from 4 percent of revenue in FY2025 to 26 percent in FY2030, while lung falls below half of group revenue from FY2028.

Over the next 18 months, revenue growth decelerates into H1 2027 and re-accelerates from H2 2027, while the EBITDA margin climbs steadily. Viewforth expects Q4 2026 revenue of about 260 (+15 percent). Growth slows to the mid-teens in H1 2027 because three effects coincide: the customer's step-down, the OPO transition and hardening comparatives. Growth then re-accelerates from H2 2027 as European heart revenue compounds and kidney supply is no longer constrained.

I have changed no forecast input, because each of the five judgements tested above sits at a defensible centre. The FY2027 EBITDA margin of 24 percent is bracketed by the two post-Q3 brokers (23.4 and 25.0 percent). The Q4 2026 revenue of about 260 sits between RedEye's 245 and DNB Carnegie's 273. The FDA dating is conservative by design, because the asymmetry of the share-price reaction argues for a base that the stock can beat. The 13 percent cost growth is the centre of a one-sided risk that I have described rather than moved. Two model items that need reconciliation are in the end-notes.

The forecasts give slower but steadier growth than the past, and the first full-cycle margin expansion.

Where my view differs from the market: Viewforth's model describes a better business, a lower earnings base and a more honest relationship between earnings and cash than the sell-side's models. On revenue, Viewforth is near consensus to FY2027 (4 percent below, because of the customer and the heart lag), 8 percent below in FY2028 (because of the FDA date) and 14 percent below in FY2029. On EBITDA, Viewforth is 14 percent below in FY2027 and FY2028, because management keeps investing. Below EBITDA lies the whole of the rest of the gap, which is where the sell-side has not done the arithmetic. On cash, Viewforth is above the two brokers who model cash, in every year.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is DNB Carnegie's: 2027 revenue of 1,276 and EBITDA of 319, on heart revenue of about 194 and lung absorbing the customer's step-down, and net income of 180 on a 15 percent tax rate and 105 of D&A. Two of judgements 1 to 3 breaking favourably at once would move my FY2027 EPS above 4.5; two breaking unfavourably would take it below 3.0, which is where the lower quartile of the EPS range sits.

Score: 70. Revenue compounding at about 23 percent for four years, an EBITDA margin rising ten points and EPS tripling from the 2026 base are a better-than-most forecast for a European listed company; the marks against are a flat EPS year in 2027, an earnings base well below consensus and a 2028 that one regulator dates.

7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Guidance offers nothing to upgrade. The probable sequence is a re-dating of the 2027 targets at or soon after the report of 28 January 2027 and a move of the United States launch date into 2028 during 2027 (the probabilities are in #4). The only "raise" available to management is a new, later set of targets, which the market would read as a reset.

Sell-side estimates will move in three directions at once, and then in one.

My probabilities of a net cut to FY2027 consensus EPS at each report are about 70 percent at the Q4 2026 report (mostly alignment of D&A and tax), 65 percent at the Q1 2027 report (the first test of lung excluding the customer, of services and of operating costs) and 55 percent at the Q2 2027 report (the abdominal margin after the manufacturing transfer, and the FDA's posture after the Day-100 meeting). FY2028 consensus is unlikely to be cut before the FDA's posture becomes visible in mid-to-late 2027; it then falls 30 to 40 percent on Viewforth's dating, with a 15 to 20 percent chance that an approval inside the brokers' window leaves FY2028 consensus intact or raised.

Revisions are already negative at every horizon. FY2027 EPS has been revised by -5, -6, -12 and -13 percent over one, three, six and twelve months; EBITDA by -3 to -7 percent; and sales by -1 to -5 percent. The revision-momentum score is -10, and the share of Buy ratings, at 100 percent, can only move one way (Pareto's target of 280 is the nearest to the price).

The sell-side describes all fifteen of the dynamics Viewforth identified but quantifies only about half, and the half it leaves unquantified lies below EBITDA. The retail investor narrative (on Placera, Avanza and in the RedEye community) is "approval dates plus quarterly sales beats". Retail investors celebrated Q3's beat on sales and net profit without adjusting for 19 of timing items and 7 of currency gains, sold hard on the customer news, and hold the 2027 targets as a promise. Five things would surprise the market, in order of size:

  1. The level of FY2027 EPS.
  2. The customer's revenue run-rate, if the fall is nearer 100 than 65.
  3. The dependence of 2028 consensus on a 2028 United States launch: RedEye's heart revenue above 500 is the single most exposed number in the public record.
  4. The multiple on Viewforth's earnings.
  5. Favourably, positive free cash flow in 2027, against the two brokers' negative numbers.

Four upgrades to Viewforth's own numbers are possible, none of them is in our forecasts or any broker's, and only one could arrive in the next six months. They are: an FDA decision earlier than late 2028 (about a 50 percent chance on my distribution, worth about 1.3 of FY2028 EPS); an outcome of the FDA pre-submission meeting (Q-sub) that confirms the liver 510(k) route without a United States clinical study (RedEye calls this upside it has not capitalised); hub throughput disclosed above about 150 EVLP runs a year (plausibly at the Q1 2027 report); and a CMS coverage route for breakthrough devices via the RAPID pathway. Each upgrade is dated, and only the Q-sub outcome might arrive within the next six months.

Where my view differs from the market. The market expects FY2026 to be beaten and reads the beat as momentum. I read the FY2026 beat as masking the cuts to the outer years, because the beat is made of tax and currency. I agree with RedEye that 2028 is the relevant investment horizon, and I disagree with RedEye's 2028 numbers.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case, with a probability of about 10 percent, is that the Q4 report delivers heart revenue above 35, lung revenue above 140 and a reaffirmation of the targets, which would hold FY2027 consensus and start the upgrade cycle early. Two Tier 2 reimbursement decisions by April 2027 plus an FDA advisory-panel date in H1 2027 would change my view: together they would reduce the FY2027 cuts from "a cut at every report" to "one alignment" and put FY2028 estimates in play upward.

Score: 24. For the next six to twelve months the direction of guidance is down or sideways, FY2027 consensus EPS must fall 25 to 35 percent toward ours, the breadth of revisions is already negative and the only favourable surprise in the window is cash; the scope for upgrades begins in H2 2027 and is keyed to a regulator.

8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and the same for key peers

Every momentum reading for Xvivo is negative or absent, except falling short interest.

Guidance: noneNo numerical guidance, and the 2027 targets are stale.
Sell-side: FScore -10; FY2027 EPS cut at every horizon; target prices -3 percent over three months; Buy share static at 100 percent.
Narrative: negative since JulyA -10 percent day on 14 July 2026 on the Q2 margin miss; the customer's platform approval in October; the Q3 beat was sold, and the shares closed lower that day.
Technical: DPrice 8.4 percent below the 200-day average (243.96); the 50-day (246.8) below the 150-day (260.1); relative strength at the 34th percentile.
Returns: -26.4% in six monthsAgainst +15.7 percent for the equal-weighted dashboard peer basket, a 42-point gap that no sector factor explains.
Short interest: 8.3%Down from about 12 percent in April, but still three times the Swedish medtech norm and a source of a squeeze on regulatory news.

Three further readings complete the picture. Returns are -9.8 percent over three months, -20.9 percent over six months and +26.9 percent over twelve months; the twelve-month figure flatters, because its base is the October 2025 low near 163. The 200-day average has risen in only six of the last twelve months. Liquidity is thin, at about USD 2.8 million a day. Finally, the co-movement data show that the stock amplified sector moves when the sector was the story (a beta of 1.62 in October 2025 and an R-squared of 33 percent in April 2026) and ignores the sector now (a beta of 0.84 and an R-squared of 9 percent).

Among peers, the consumables sector has de-rated together, and momentum is split by delivery. Fourteen of seventeen rated dashboard peers sit in the bottom decile of their own ten-year valuation history, so the valuation A is the sector's grade, not Xvivo's distinction. Bonesupport is the sector's live beat-and-raise on a payment decision, with 39 percent growth and a 34 percent adjusted EBIT margin in Q3 2026, and it is the comparator that the same Nordic investor base will set against Xvivo's cutting cycle. Getinge beat on Q3 margins and called Paragonix "outstanding", which supports the demand side of Xvivo's thesis but says nothing about Xvivo's margins. Outside the dashboard, the two perfusion read-acrosses are TransMedics and Terumo. TransMedics reports Q3 on 5 November 2026; its last two results days each moved its shares by 25 percent or more, and its January 2025 short-seller episode took its shares down 49 percent in three months and compressed Xvivo's multiple in sympathy. Terumo raised guidance in August 2026, with Organ Technologies growing 50 percent against a 20 percent margin target.

Inference and so-what: the re-rating of Xvivo's shares is entirely in the hands of the company and the FDA. The one peer that shows what the market pays for delivery, Bonesupport, is doing what Xvivo cannot do: beating and raising numerical guidance. Xvivo's idiosyncrasy cuts both ways, because a sector recovery is worth perhaps only 5 to 8 percent to Xvivo in expectation.

Where my view differs from the market. The market reads the twelve-month return (+26.9 percent) and the falling short interest as a bottom. I read the six-month underperformance against the peer basket and the structure of the moving averages as a stock still in a downtrend, whose next two reports are more likely to cut estimates than to confirm them. I agree that short interest at 8.3 percent is fuel for a discontinuous move on good regulatory news.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that momentum indicators lag at inflections, and that the stock is 39 percent above its 52-week low with its two largest overhangs (the CE mark and the PMA acceptance) removed. Two events would change my view: a close above the 200-day average held through the Q4 report, or a TransMedics Q3 report on 5 November that shows pricing pushback and volume pressure in United States heart, which would strengthen the narrative for Xvivo's heart entry.

Score: 20. Sell-side momentum F, technical momentum D, a narrative that sold a beat, and no guidance to carry momentum, against a sector whose leaders (Bonesupport, Getinge) are in the opposite cycle; the only positive readings are falling short interest and idiosyncratic sensitivity to good regulatory news.

9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

The case is simple in words (perfusion adoption plus two launches) but not simple in numbers. Three operating drivers and one currency carry almost the whole of the FY2027 variance: European heart revenue, lung revenue net of a customer whose transition is undisclosed, management's discretionary cost build, and the krona. One regulator's date carries most of the FY2028 variance. That concentration is extreme by peer standards: greater than Ambu's, and similar to Bonesupport's dependence on one product and one payment decision. The concentration falls only by FY2029, when five drivers of comparable size share the growth. On the positive side, the business can be monitored with about a dozen numbers a quarter.

The range of outcomes over 18 months is wide, and for EPS it is skewed to the downside.

  • FY2027 revenue: 1,090 to 1,230 around 1,162, with a mild negative skew. The customer and the OPO transition have concrete downsides, and heart's upside is capped by the December 2026 start of CE-marked sales and by reimbursement calendars.
  • FY2027 EBITDA margin: 21 to 27 percent around 24, symmetric. Both tails depend on discretionary spending.
  • FY2027 EPS: 2.1 to 5.6 around 3.8, with a negative skew. The krona's consensus path and an amortisation line already revised up once both point down. The one favourable surprise available below EBITDA, the recognition of United States deferred tax assets, needs United States profits that are not in prospect before 2029.

I put about 25 percent probability on FY2027 EPS at or below 3.0, 50 percent between 3.0 and 4.5, and 25 percent above 4.5; only the upper decile exceeds consensus. In share-price terms, the 18-month range that the market itself implies runs from about 110 (20x Viewforth's 24-month-forward EPS of 5.6) to about 400 (the five-year median multiple of 45x on consensus EPS), which is wider than for any peer on the dashboard.

The 2027 forecast rests about 70 percent on demonstrated strengths, and from 2028 the proportions reverse. In 2027, the demonstrated strengths are the lung franchise, the European clinical network and cost discipline when management chooses it; the strengths still to be acquired (about 30 percent) are Tier 2 reimbursement in at least two countries, a clean manufacturing transfer and a services unit that stops losing money. From 2028, most of the forecast rests on strengths still to be acquired: United States commercial execution against TransMedics, which has a 26 percent share of United States heart, lung and liver transplants and 22 aircraft, and a liver route that the FDA has not confirmed.

The earnings thesis also rests on four numbers that the company does not disclose: the cost build behind each milestone, the amortisation each approval triggers, the tax rate and the currency effect. Each of the four has moved EPS by more than the milestones in at least one of the last three years, which is why DNB Carnegie and RedEye differ by 80 percent on 2027 net income on sales that differ by only 10 percent.

The risks are known, dated and concentrated, but they arrive suddenly, and the share price reacts to misses two to three times as strongly as to beats.

-30%in one day, on the Q2 2025 destocking
-25%on the CE-mark delay
-64%across 2025
-10%on 14 July 2026, on the Q2 margin miss
+15%on the Q4 2025 margin beat

Regulatory letters are price-sensitive under Swedish rules and will arrive unscheduled: a Day-100 communication in early January 2027; possibly a major-deficiency letter, which 92 percent of the 2026 PMA cohort received; and possibly an advisory-panel listing. By contrast, the OPO transition and the customer's drawdown are trackable only through segment lines, after the fact. The channels through which perception moves the shares are unusually large for a company of this quality: Xvivo is small, thinly traded, shorted, unanimously rated Buy, read across from a volatile United States bellwether and listed in one of the most rate-sensitive developed economies.

Cyclicality is not the risk, but Xvivo fits two of the sector's characteristic failure patterns and two of its outperformance patterns at once. Transplant demand is non-cyclical and the balance sheet is unlevered.

  • Failure pattern 1: the capitalised-cost "false friend". A reassuring EBITDA margin is built on capitalised development; the Q3 2026 EPS of 1.42 included about 0.22 of currency gains, 8.5 of lease recognition and about 10 of customer inventory.
  • Failure pattern 2: the single-customer, slipped-date underperformer. Xvivo's own 2025 is the example.
  • Outperformance pattern 1: an approval or payment decision that creates the market a year later, as in Bonesupport's SOLARIO and Medicare cycle.
  • Outperformance pattern 2: worries clearing at a range low through multiple expansion, as European medtech showed after major sell-offs.

Vitrolife, which took 9.7 billion of impairments after serial target misses, is the precedent for what the sector does to a company that repeatedly misses its own targets. Xvivo's 2027 targets follow the Vitrolife pattern in guidance terms; so far, the clinical record has redeemed them in the Bonesupport pattern.

Five sudden, large fundamental risks exist; none threatens survival, and two would break the 2028 numbers.

A dozen readings across the next two reports (28 January and late April 2027) will show which side of the range the year is on. Beyond the readings in the table, the Q4 report should confirm that the first CE-marked heart invoices were issued in December 2026.

Where my view differs from the market. The market and the brokers describe the case as a story of margin trajectory plus catalysts, with known risks. I describe it as a case in which about half of the FY2027 EPS range lies below the gross-profit line, and in which the price already discounts more than the brokers' numbers do but less than Viewforth's numbers do. Position sizing should assume that a drawdown of a third is ordinary for this stock, because the record shows that it is.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the business is more forecastable than its peers (its segment disclosure is better than Ambu's or TransMedics'), that the balance sheet removes solvency risk and that the strategic floor bounds the downside. Two disclosures would change my view: numerical guidance or an EBITDA-to-EPS bridge from the company, which would halve the uncertainty below EBITDA, or a disclosed revenue run-rate for the customer.

Score: 28. A simple story with concentrated, dated and trackable drivers, but an EPS cone of plus or minus 45 percent, binary regulatory dates that arrive unscheduled, a record of -25 to -30 percent days, an unhedged currency and a crowded, illiquid, unanimously rated security make it riskier than most listed European companies.

10Where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle

The business confirms the dashboard's "Turning/Inflecting" placement, but the earnings narrative does not. The business evidence for turning is strong: revenue growth went from -0.6 percent in Q4 2025 to +34 percent; the two largest overhangs (European heart approval and the FDA's acceptance of the file) cleared in the last three months; operating cash flow has been positive for four quarters; and the structural demand force is strengthening. The earnings evidence points the other way: reported EPS will be flat in FY2027; consensus has cut the near years and raised the far year; the company's targets are about to be re-dated; and reported growth is at its most flattering point and about to decelerate on arithmetic alone, because of the Q3 timing items, the customer and comparatives of +10 to +34 percent from Q1 2027.

The thesis has broadened, from a lung consumables story to an all-organ platform with a European heart launch and a United States filing, but the numbers have not yet reinforced the broader thesis. The multiple has done the bottoming. The current regime of 25 to 35x on consensus has lasted 19 months and is the lowest in ten years; it followed a 2023 regime of 38 to 53x, when revenue growth of 44 percent was believed, and a 2024 regime of 46 to 66x, when margins expanded too.

My placement: turning up on the business, bottoming on the multiple, and in a stalling interlude in earnings momentum that the market has priced into the multiple but not into the numbers. In the lifecycle sequence used here (bottoming, turning up, thesis broadening, reinforcing, stalling), the stock sits between "turning up" and "thesis broadening", and the step to "reinforcing" has a date: the first commercial heart quarters (Q1 to Q2 2027) and the FDA's posture (H2 2027). The risk is a "stalling" reading for two to three quarters as FY2027 consensus comes down. The opportunity is that the phase after the stall has a known trigger, and the security attached to it is under-owned, thinly covered and still shorted.

Where my view differs from the market. Together, the dashboard's A for valuation and F for sell-side momentum describe a bottoming stock. On Viewforth's earnings the valuation leg is a C (mid-range) and the momentum leg is an F, which describes a stock that is still turning rather than one that has turned. The sell-side's 100 percent Buy ratings and the strategic-floor argument describe a "reinforcing" stock; the quarterly results do not yet.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the market has already done the earnings work through the multiple (the 26 percent six-month fall against a rising peer basket), and that the next estimate cut will be the last. Q1 2027 heart revenue above 32 with two Tier 2 decisions would move my placement toward "reinforcing". Lung revenue below 130, with services still loss-making and a reaffirmation of the targets that defers the reset to January 2028, would move my placement toward "stalling".

Score: 48. The business is turning up with the structural force behind it and two overhangs cleared, but the earnings narrative faces a stall of two to three quarters and the step to reinforcing is dated by a regulator, which puts the stock in the middle of the pack on lifecycle attractiveness today and higher by mid-2027 if the quarters cooperate.

11The fair multiple

Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Turning/Inflecting stock is 53.94x two-year-forward earnings, 111 percent above today's multiple on consensus EPS (25.5x) and 35 percent above today's multiple on Viewforth's EPS (39.9x). The guideline is the 60th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E, with outlier months excluded. The ten-year bands are 35.1x (10th percentile, "crash"), 45.1x (35th, "conservative"), 50.2x (median, "prudent"), 60.7x (75th, "defendable") and 72.0x (90th, "mania").

The guideline multiple fairly describes where the stock trades when its thesis is reinforcing, but it is generous for the 18-month horizon, for four reasons. The stock traded at 46 to 66x in 2024, when revenue growth of 38 percent was believed and margins were expanding, and it can trade there again once United States heart approval is in hand and consensus has reset to a base the company beats. Within 18 months, however:

  1. Viewforth's own guideline principle argues for less. A stock in the turning-up phase, where forecasts are more uncertain, earns the lower part of its range, and the next four quarters carry a flat EPS year and a downgrade cycle.
  2. The live peer argues for less. Bonesupport, the sector's delivering single-product medtech in a beat-and-raise cycle with 30 percent growth and EBITDA margins of 29 to 35 percent, trades at 33.4x on the dashboard's forward P/E measure, the same measure that gives Xvivo 25.5x on consensus. On Viewforth's EPS Xvivo already trades at 39.9x with a flat year ahead, so a 54x multiple would be a 60 percent premium to the best-delivering comparator.
  3. The market regime argues for less. A discount-rate shock and a market that "refuses re-ratings" argue against assuming the top half of any range within 18 months.
  4. The earnings base makes the re-rating a two-step move. The market currently capitalises consensus EPS at 25.5x. The re-rating that the guideline requires is not from 25.5x to 54x on the same earnings; it is from 39.9x to 54x on earnings 35 to 40 percent lower than the market currently believes. The earnings must reset first, and only then can the multiple re-rate.

My central fair multiple for March 2028 is therefore 45x, the 35th-percentile "conservative" band. That band matches the 2023 regime, when growth was believed but margins were not yet proven. The guideline 54x is the multiple the stock earns on a clean FDA path with European heart delivering; 35x (the 10th percentile) is the fair level if the FDA requests more data or the customer transition runs fast. For the three-year horizon to September 2029, with United States heart revenue in the numbers and the margin expansion a year into delivery, the guideline is my central case.

Where my view differs from the market. The sell-side justifies a premium multiple by the strategic-buyer transactions, and RedEye does so in every note. I accept the floor and reject the ceiling: an acquirer's multiple of sales bounds how far the shares can fall, but it says nothing about what a public-market holder will pay in 2028 for 2029 earnings. The market reads the stock as at its valuation floor; on Viewforth's earnings it is not. The support of a "trough valuation" therefore disappears at the same moment as the estimates fall, unless the multiple re-rates for the lower base. That re-rating for a lower base is precisely the pattern of worries clearing at a range low, which European medtech has shown and which this stock showed in 2023.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case for the full guideline at 18 months is that the stock traded at 45 to 53x through 2023 on a lung-only story with EBITDA margins of 13 to 14 percent; an all-organ story with margins of 24 to 27 percent and United States heart approval in sight deserves more, and 8.3 percent short interest means that the move, when it comes, will be discontinuous. An FDA advisory-panel date or approvable letter in 2027, or FY2027 heart revenue at the sell-side's 180 to 194, would move my central multiple up to the guideline within 18 months. A deficiency letter requiring new data, or a re-dating of the 2027 targets accompanied by lung revenue below 130, would move it down to 35x.

Score: 55. The guideline multiple of 53.94x is 111 percent above today's consensus-based multiple and 35 percent above the multiple on our earnings, which is a larger re-rating opportunity than most European companies offer; it is tempered because the stock is already mid-range on the earnings we believe, a flat EPS year precedes the re-rating, and the delivering peer trades 60 percent cheaper.

12Total shareholder return, via the Dupont framework

At the guideline fair multiple, the model gives a total return of +130.3 percent to 31 March 2028 and +240.6 percent to 30 September 2029, with no contribution from dividends. From a share price of 223.40 (22 October 2026) and a 24-month-forward P/E of 39.9x on the model's EPS, the guideline 53.94x is reached at the 18-month point. The value per share is 514.50 at 31 March 2028 (+78.8 percent annualised) and 760.95 at 30 September 2029 (+51.8 percent annualised). Dividends contribute nothing at either horizon, because none is paid or modelled and the balance sheet funds the launches. The template's own split of this return is inconsistent with the model's rising EPS path; the end-notes explain it, and my decomposition follows.

On 24-month-forward EPS, roughly two-thirds of the 18-month return and three-quarters of the three-year return come from earnings growth that is already in forecasts 35 to 40 percent below consensus. The multiple supplies about a third and a quarter respectively, in compound terms. Today, 223.4 equals 39.9x times 5.60, a blend of FY2027 EPS of 3.82 and FY2028 EPS of 6.07. At 31 March 2028, 514.5 equals 53.94x times 9.54, a blend of FY2029 EPS of 8.75 and FY2030 EPS of 12.18. At 30 September 2029, 760.95 equals 53.94x times 14.11, which uses FY2030 and the model's extension beyond it.

The earnings leg needs neither the company's 2027 targets nor the sell-side's 2028 United States launch. The rise in 24-month-forward EPS from 5.6 to 9.5 comes from the European heart ramp (155 to 275 to 420), kidney supply no longer being constrained, the abdominal margin recovering on unit cost, the EBITDA margin rising from 24 to 29.5 percent as the cost base grows more slowly than revenue from 2028, and the first United States heart revenue (about 90 in 2029), net of 185 of amortisation and a 22 percent tax rate.

The multiple leg needs three things in sequence, and it is a re-rating for lower earnings, which is why #11 haircuts it for the 18-month horizon. First, FY2027 consensus must reset to a base the company can beat, which the cuts of the next four reports will achieve. Second, the CE-marked heart quarters must compound visibly from Q1 2027. Third, the FDA's posture must be benign by mid-to-late 2027.

The return at other multiples and earnings paths, for March 2028.

The probability-weighted 18-month return is about +70 to +80 percent, with a 25 percent probability of a loss of a quarter to a half. The weights are roughly a quarter on the lower two rows, a half on my central case and a quarter on the guideline. The favourable skew comes from the convexity of the multiple on a clean regulatory path and from a strategic floor (the sector pays 11 to 20x sales for such assets in private transactions), not from the earnings alone. The three-year return at the guideline (+241 percent) needs United States heart revenue of about 90 in 2029 and 190 in 2030 and an EBITDA margin near 30 percent; at 45x, the three-year return is about +185 percent.

Where my view differs from the market. The sell-side's target prices (280 to 360) imply 25 to 60 percent upside on the brokers' earnings. The model implies more upside on lower earnings, because it pays a higher multiple over a longer horizon. The market's framework capitalises next year's EPS; the return case here capitalises 2029 to 2030 EPS at a multiple the stock last earned in 2024. The return case is therefore a longer-duration bet than the sell-side's and more exposed to the discount-rate regime.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is the regime: a market that refuses re-ratings holds the stock at 25 to 40x for the whole horizon, in which case the return is the earnings leg alone, +8 to +70 percent over 18 months depending on whose EPS the market capitalises. An FDA decision inside 2027 would change my view upward, because it would pull the guideline multiple into the 18-month window and lift FY2028 EPS by about 1.3. A Q1 2027 report that cuts FY2027 estimates without delivering heart evidence would change my view downward, because it would push the re-rating out by two quarters and deepen the drawdown first.

Score: 66. A total return of +130 percent over 18 months and +241 percent over three years at the guideline, and about +90 and +185 percent at my central multiple, ranks high among European listed companies; it is held back from the top decile by a 25 percent probability of a loss of a quarter to a half in the same window, a zero cash-return leg, and a re-rating that must be earned on an earnings base the market has not yet accepted.

13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Over three years, Xvivo is a strong business case that needs neither the company's own targets nor the sell-side's dates. Xvivo is the only listed all-organ machine-perfusion platform. It has a lung franchise as well defended as any consumables business in European medtech, a heart system with the category's best evidence at a third of the incumbent's price, a self-funding balance sheet, and a management that delivers clinical and regulatory milestones but is slow commercially. The demand behind Xvivo is structural, strengthening and independent of the company. The three-year case is revenue compounding at about 23 percent, an EBITDA margin rising ten points, EPS tripling from the 2026 base and free cash flow turning positive for the first time, all of it below consensus.

Over the next six to twelve months, the case is the reverse. Xvivo faces a flat EPS year that the market has not modelled, a 25 to 35 percent cut to FY2027 consensus delivered in instalments, a re-dating of the 2027 targets, a customer stepping down by an undisclosed amount, and a share price that is cheap on the market's earnings and mid-range on Viewforth's. Both valuations cannot hold. The resolution is that the market's EPS converges on Viewforth's, while the evidence that re-rates the stock (commercial European heart quarters from Q1 2027, Tier 2 reimbursement, the liver 510(k) submission and the FDA's posture by mid-2027) arrives afterward.

The return is mostly earnings, and the skew is favourable. The return at the guideline fair multiple (+130 percent to March 2028; +241 percent to September 2029) is mostly earnings growth already in Viewforth's forecasts, plus a re-rating from 40x to 54x that the stock earns only once consensus has reset and the heart leg is visible. My central multiple gives about +90 percent over 18 months, and the fair trough is 37 to 50 percent below the price. The skew of fundamental outcomes is favourable over two to three years (cash, a conservatively dated FDA decision and a strategic floor), while the skew of guidance and sell-side revisions is unfavourable over the next two to three reports. The setup improves with each estimate cut.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: B. A structural, externally driven demand inflection and the company's largest-ever product launch are strong and dated forces. They are held below A by the 2027 transition year, in which a customer's insourcing and management's spending neutralise both forces in the reported numbers.

Foundations' Robustness: C. The lung franchise, the clinical record and the balance sheet are top-quartile; returns on capital near 4 percent, an earnings base flattered by capitalisation, contested abdominal pricing, a loss-making services node and an unproven United States commercial organisation are not.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. The case straddles two Viewforth setups. The first, "Major CfC clearing in an MQ non-cyclical business on a Q1 multiple", fits on consensus earnings but not on Viewforth's. The second, "Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU", fits for 2028 to 2030, while 2027 is a stall. A case that sits on a Q1 multiple only on earnings that Viewforth thinks are wrong is not a crisp fit.

Case Riskiness: D. The case is simple in words but not in numbers, with an EPS cone of plus or minus 45 percent, binary regulatory dates, an unhedged krona, a record of -25 to -30 percent days and a crowded, illiquid security, so the drawdown to size for is a third.

Sources and definitions.

  1. "Consensus" is the FactSet median of 22 October 2026. Its latest estimate date is 6 October 2026, so it predates the Q3 2026 report. "Post-Q3" refers to the DNB Carnegie and RedEye notes of 23 October 2026, from the only two brokers to have updated since the report.
  2. "Our forecasts" and "Viewforth's model" are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2. The latest Earnings Review in the research folder covers the September 2026 quarter, which resolves the caution about data currency in the instruction.
  3. FY2025 EPS of 0.88 is on the model's own definition; the brokers'-basis actual is 1.03. FY2029 consensus rests on two brokers and is not a consensus in any useful sense.
  4. The source draft's summary gave FY2026 free cash flow as about -8; the forecast table, used throughout this memo, gives -3.
  5. The model has been through three rounds of review. The fourth set of review comments corrected two factual errors in the second set: a misread nine-month tax rate, and a working-capital release that FactSet's quarterly series invented (FactSet shows working capital at 5.6 percent of sales; the true figure is 20 to 30 percent). The fair-trough arithmetic in #12 comes from the first and fourth sets.

Items flagged for the Financial Analyst to reconcile, which do not change the conclusions.

  1. Net cash. The model's year-end net cash (-158.7 for FY2026 and -143.5 for FY2027) cannot be reconciled with reported net cash of 193 at 30 September 2026 and free cash flow near zero in Q4. The gap of about 350 sits in an opening balance or a debt definition, and it should be fixed before any enterprise-value multiple uses the model's net cash. The gap does not affect the total shareholder return, which has no dividend leg.
  2. The template's split of total shareholder return. The template's own Dupont sheet attributes +176.1 percent to the multiple and -16.6 percent to earnings over 18 months, and +120.5 percent and +54.5 percent over three years. The legs multiply to the stated totals, but a negative 18-month earnings leg cannot be squared with the model's rising EPS path. I therefore read the template's split as resting on a different earnings base, and I give my own decomposition in #12.

Glossary of acronyms and terms.

CE mark
The European Union conformity marking required to sell a medical device commercially in Europe
CFO
Chief financial officer
CMS
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the United States federal health-insurance agency
Continued Access Protocol
An FDA arrangement that lets trial sites keep using a device while its approval application is reviewed
Day-100 meeting
The FDA's meeting with the applicant about 100 days into a premarket approval review
DCD
Donation after circulatory death
Derogation
Special national permission to use a device before it carries the CE mark
ECMO
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
EVLP
Ex vivo lung perfusion: assessing and treating a donor lung outside the body before transplant
NICE
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (United Kingdom)
NRP
Normothermic regional perfusion: restoring warm blood flow to organs inside the donor after death
OCS
Organ Care System, TransMedics' warm-perfusion platform
OPO
Organ procurement organisation
PMA
Premarket approval, the FDA's approval route for high-risk devices
Q-sub
An FDA pre-submission meeting that gives feedback before a formal filing
510(k)
An FDA clearance route for a device shown to be substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate device
Tier 2
In the heart rollout, the second tier of European countries for reimbursement; in the CMS rule, Tier 3 is the lowest-performing group of OPOs
XPS, STEEN, Perfadex
Xvivo's lung-perfusion machine, its warm lung-perfusion fluid and its cold lung-preservation fluid

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • Consensus net income for FY2026 is 102.76, +270.2% against 27.76 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +22.5%.
  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 3.38, +283.0% against 0.88 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +22.5%.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Amortisation of acquired intangibles over the last twelve months: -35.8 before tax (-1.13 per share); our model's FY2025 history does not exclude it (its EBITA equals EBIT). Brokers' adjusted figures often exclude it.
  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.
